questions.q: What is the birth year and birthplace of the author vlxj otkgr as given in the "Before You Read" section?
questions.a: The author vlxj otkgr was born in 1946 in Prayagraj (इलाहाबाद), Uttar Pradesh. A wrong answer (e.g., 1950, Delhi) reveals the student has not read the biographical note carefully or is confusing this author with another — a common error when multiple authors are studied in quick succession.

questions.q: In your own words, explain why the author's experience in journalism and radio (आकाशवाणी) is relevant to understanding the language and themes of his stories.
questions.a: Journalism and radio demand concise, colloquial, and immediately engaging language to reach a broad audience; this explains the "सरल, बोलचाल की भाषा, व्यंग्यात्मक शैली" (simple, colloquial language, satirical style) noted in the text. A wrong answer that says "it doesn't matter" or "he wrote for children" misses the direct link between professional writing constraints and literary craft — a misconception that biography is separate from textual analysis.

questions.q: Based on the one-paragraph summary of 'ksj provided in the "Before You Read" section, identify the central metaphor and state what social reality it critiques.
questions.a: The central metaphor is the 'ksj (well) whose mouth is covered by a lid — it represents the common citizen whose voice is silenced by authoritarian power. The story critiques a system where the state (जादूगर/शासक) manipulates fear and propaganda to make people voluntarily surrender their agency. A wrong answer that focuses only on the literal well or the magician's tricks shows inability to move from plot summary to allegorical reading.

questions.q: Compare the summaries of igpku and pkj gkFk. What common pattern of power abuse do they share, and how does the scale differ?
questions.a: Both depict a ruler/authority figure (जादूगर in igpku, फ़कीर/सेठ in pkj gkFk) who exploits the labour and bodies of the powerless (subjects, workers) to maintain control. The difference: igpku shows systemic, state-level totalitarianism (whole population enslaved), while pkj gkFk shows feudal/economic exploitation at a village/household level. A wrong answer that treats them as unrelated stories misses the chapter's structural design — four variations on the same theme of power and resistance.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: "The vocabulary list (लहकना, मचिया हिवना, फ़क़ीर, फ़कत, म्यान) is merely a dictionary aid and not necessary for thematic understanding." Defend your position with evidence from the story summaries.
questions.a: The claim is false. Each term is a cultural signpost: लहकना and मचिया हिवना (dialect words) ground the stories in rural Awadhi/Bhojpuri speech, signalling class and region; फ़क़ीर and फ़कत appear in pkj gkFk and lk>k where religious/economic hypocrisy is central; म्यान (scabbard) in lk>k hints at hidden violence. Ignoring them flattens the text's socio-linguistic texture. A student who agrees with the claim treats vocabulary as decoration, not as a thematic code.

questions.q: Create a one-sentence "back-cover blurb" for the entire chapter (all four stories) that would attract a Class 12 reader, using at least three keywords from the "Before You Read" section.
questions.a: Example: "Four razor-sharp satires — a well that swallows dissent, a magician who enslaves a kingdom with fear, a fakir who trades four legs for human labour, and a servant who outwits his master's cruelty — expose how power devours the powerless, all told in the earthy, ironic voice of a journalist-turned-storyteller." A weak blurb that merely lists titles or uses generic praise ("interesting stories") shows the student hasn't synthesized the thematic core.
